Physiology-04.question: ১) Which is called master gland?
Physiology-04.exp:
The anterior pituitary gland (adenohypophysis) is called the master gland because it secretes several tropic hormones that regulate the functions of other endocrine glands.

Hormones secreted by anterior pituitary:

  • TSH → Stimulates thyroid gland

  • ACTH → Stimulates adrenal cortex

  • FSH & LH → Regulate gonads

  • GH → Growth and metabolism

  • Prolactin → Milk production

Other options:

  • Posterior pituitary → Stores and releases ADH and oxytocin (produced by hypothalamus)

  • Hypothalamus → Controls pituitary function and maintains endocrine regulation

  • Pancreas → Produces insulin and glucagon

Exam pearl:

  • Master gland → Anterior pituitary

  • Master controller of endocrine system → Hypothalamus

  • Posterior pituitary hormones → ADH + Oxytocin

Physiology-04.question: ২) Which hormone has receptor on nucleus?
Physiology-04.exp:
Steroid hormones have intracellular receptors, mainly located in the cytoplasm or nucleus. The hormone–receptor complex enters the nucleus and binds to DNA to regulate gene transcription.

Examples:

  • Cortisol

  • Aldosterone

  • Estrogen

  • Testosterone

  • Progesterone

Other options:

  • Thyroid hormones → Also act through nuclear receptors (important exception)

  • Protein & polypeptide hormones → Act through cell membrane receptors

  • Catecholamines → Act through cell membrane receptors (GPCRs)

Note: If the question asks broadly “which hormone has receptor on nucleus,” both steroid and thyroid hormones are correct. In most physiology MCQs, steroid hormone is the expected answer.

Exam pearl:

  • Nuclear receptor → Steroid hormones + Thyroid hormones

  • Membrane receptor → Peptide hormones + Catecholamines

Physiology-04.question: ৩) Which hormone is amine by chemical structure?
৪) Which promotes development of female breast & secretion of milk?
৫) Which promotes deposition of calcium in the bone?
৬) Which stimulates secretion of uterine milk?
৭) Which of the following factor inhibits GH secretion?
৮) Excess GH secretion during childhood may result in
Physiology-04.exp:
Excess secretion of growth hormone (GH) during childhood (before closure of epiphyseal plates) causes gigantism. It leads to excessive growth of long bones and increased height.

GH excess effects:

  • Childhood → Gigantism (linear growth ↑)

  • Adult → Acromegaly (epiphyseal plates already closed; enlargement of hands, feet, jaw, facial bones)

Other options:

  • Acromegaly → Excess GH after epiphyseal closure

  • Dwarfism → Usually due to GH deficiency in childhood

  • Diabetes insipidus (DI) → Due to ADH deficiency or renal resistance to ADH

Exam pearl:

  • GH excess before puberty → Gigantism

  • GH excess after puberty → Acromegaly

  • GH deficiency in childhood → Pituitary dwarfism

Physiology-04.question: ৯) Catecholamines excludes
Physiology-04.exp:
Catecholamines are hormones/neurotransmitters derived from tyrosine and contain a catechol ring with an amine group.

Catecholamines include:

  • Epinephrine (adrenaline)

  • Norepinephrine (noradrenaline)

  • Dopamine

Neurotensin is a neuropeptide, not a catecholamine.

Exam pearl:

  • Catecholamines → Dopamine → Norepinephrine → Epinephrine

  • Derived from tyrosine

  • Neurotensin → Peptide neurotransmitter/hormone

Physiology-04.question: ১০) Amino acid required for thyroid hormone synthesis
১১) Hypoglycemia mostly affects which system?
Physiology-04.exp:
Hypoglycemia mainly affects the nervous system because the brain depends heavily on glucose as its primary energy source and has limited glucose storage.

Low blood glucose causes neuroglycopenic symptoms such as:

  • Confusion

  • Difficulty concentrating

  • Drowsiness

  • Seizures

  • Loss of consciousness (coma in severe cases)

It also produces autonomic symptoms due to counter-regulatory hormone release:

  • Sweating

  • Tremor

  • Palpitations

Other systems are less primarily affected:

  • Cardiovascular → May show tachycardia due to sympathetic activation

  • Respiratory → Not a major target

  • GIT → Not primarily affected

Exam pearl:

  • Most vulnerable organ in hypoglycemia → Brain (Nervous system)

  • Severe hypoglycemia → Seizure, coma, irreversible brain injury

Physiology-04.question: ১২) Thyroid hormone increases all of the following except
১৩) Non classical site of insulin receptor
Physiology-04.exp:
The classical insulin receptor sites are mainly found in:

  • Liver

  • Skeletal muscle

  • Adipose tissue

These are the major target tissues responsible for insulin’s metabolic actions.

Lymphocytes have insulin receptors but are considered a non-classical site because insulin is not primarily involved in regulating glucose metabolism in these cells.

Functions of insulin:

  • Liver → ↓ gluconeogenesis, ↑ glycogenesis

  • Muscle → ↑ glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis

  • Fat cells → ↑ glucose uptake and fat storage

Exam pearl:

  • Classical insulin target tissues → Liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue

  • Non-classical insulin receptor site → Lymphocytes

Physiology-04.question: ১৪) Which factor inhibits hypothalamus for thyroid hormone synthesis?
Physiology-04.exp:
Leptin inhibits the hypothalamus and decreases thyroid hormone synthesis by reducing the activity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid (HPT) axis.

The pathway:
Hypothalamus (TRH) → Anterior pituitary (TSH) → Thyroid gland (T3/T4)

Factors affecting thyroid hormone synthesis:

  • Leptin → Inhibits hypothalamic TRH secretion (negative regulation)

  • Stress → Usually suppresses thyroid axis indirectly, but not the best answer here

  • Low BMR → Result of low thyroid hormone, not a direct inhibitor

  • MSH → Mainly involved in pigmentation and appetite regulation, not thyroid hormone control

Exam pearl:

  • Leptin → stimulates TRH under normal nutritional state but can regulate thyroid axis

  • High thyroid hormone (T3/T4) → inhibits TRH and TSH by negative feedback

  • HPT axis: TRH → TSH → T3/T4

Physiology-04.question: ১৫) Cardinal features of Conn's syndrome excludes
Physiology-04.exp:
Conn’s syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is caused by excessive secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex.

Excess aldosterone causes:

  • Hypertension due to increased sodium and water retention

  • Hypokalemia due to increased potassium excretion

  • Metabolic alkalosis due to increased hydrogen ion excretion

  • Muscular weakness due to hypokalemia

Hyperkalemia is not a feature; it is the opposite of what occurs in Conn’s syndrome.

Exam pearl:

  • Conn’s syndrome = Hypertension + Hypokalemia + Metabolic alkalosis

  • Aldosterone acts on principal cells → Na⁺ retention + K⁺ loss

  • Aldosterone acts on intercalated cells → H⁺ loss → alkalosis

Physiology-04.question: ১৬) Which one is neuroendocrine structure?
Physiology-04.exp:
The hypothalamus is a neuroendocrine structure because it links the nervous system with the endocrine system. It contains neurosecretory neurons that produce hormones and regulate pituitary gland function.

Functions:

  • Produces TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine

  • Produces ADH and oxytocin (stored and released from posterior pituitary)

  • Controls the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal system

Other options:

  • Adrenal cortex → Endocrine gland producing steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone)

  • Pancreas → Endocrine organ producing insulin and glucagon

  • Parathyroid → Endocrine gland producing PTH

Exam pearl:

  • Neuroendocrine link → Hypothalamus

  • Master gland → Anterior pituitary

  • Hypothalamus controls pituitary via releasing and inhibiting hormones

Physiology-04.question: ১৭) Thyroid hormone deficiency in children results in
Physiology-04.exp:
Thyroid hormone deficiency in children causes cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism). Thyroid hormones are essential for normal brain development, growth, and skeletal maturation during childhood.

Features of cretinism:

  • Mental retardation (if untreated)

  • Short stature

  • Delayed bone development

  • Developmental delay

Other options:

  • Graves’ disease → Hyperthyroidism due to TSH receptor antibodies

  • Myxedema → Severe hypothyroidism in adults

  • None of them → Incorrect because cretinism is the correct condition

Exam pearl:

  • Childhood hypothyroidism → Cretinism

  • Adult hypothyroidism → Myxedema

  • Hyperthyroidism → Graves’ disease (common cause)

Physiology-04.question: ১৮) Sites of action of PTH excludes
১৯) Receptors of calcitonin are found in
Physiology-04.exp:
Calcitonin receptors are mainly found on osteoclasts and kidney cells. Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity and increasing calcium deposition in bone. It also acts on the kidney to influence calcium and phosphate handling.

Functions of calcitonin:

  • ↓ Osteoclast activity → ↓ bone resorption

  • ↑ Calcium deposition in bone

  • ↓ Serum calcium level

Other options:

  • Liver → Not a major target organ for calcitonin

  • Intestine → No significant direct calcitonin receptor action

  • Lung → Not a target site

Exam pearl:

  • Calcitonin receptor → Osteoclast + Kidney

  • Calcitonin → Decreases blood Ca²⁺

  • PTH → Increases blood Ca²⁺

Physiology-04.question: ২০) Most common form of calcium is
Physiology-04.exp:
In plasma, calcium exists in three forms:

  1. Protein-bound calcium → about 40% (most abundant form)

    • Mainly bound to albumin

  2. Ionized (free) calcium → about 50% (biologically active form)

  3. Calcium complexed to anions → about 10%

    • Bound with phosphate, citrate, bicarbonate, etc.

Although ionized calcium is the physiologically active form, the most common form of calcium in plasma is protein-bound calcium.

Exam pearl:

  • Most abundant plasma calcium → Protein-bound calcium (~40%)

  • Active form → Ionized calcium (~50%)

  • Low albumin → decreases total serum calcium but ionized calcium may remain normal

Physiology-04.question: ২১) Ovarian hormone
Physiology-04.exp:
The ovary produces several hormones, including:

  • Estrogen → Produced mainly by ovarian follicles; responsible for female secondary sexual characteristics and endometrial proliferation

  • Progesterone → Produced mainly by the corpus luteum; prepares and maintains the endometrium for pregnancy

  • Relaxin → Produced by the corpus luteum (and later placenta); helps in pregnancy by relaxing pelvic ligaments and softening the cervix

Therefore, all of the listed hormones are ovarian hormones.

Exam pearl:

  • Major ovarian hormones → Estrogen + Progesterone + Relaxin

  • Corpus luteum → Progesterone + Relaxin

  • Follicle → Mainly Estrogen

Physiology-04.question: ২২) Tetany occurs when plasma calcium level falls below …mg/dl
Physiology-04.exp:
Tetany occurs when plasma ionized calcium level falls significantly, usually when serum calcium falls below about 5 mg/dL.

Low calcium increases neuromuscular excitability by reducing the threshold for nerve and muscle action potentials, causing:

  • Muscle spasms

  • Carpopedal spasm

  • Paresthesia

  • Laryngospasm (severe cases)

Normal total serum calcium:

  • Approximately 8.5–10.5 mg/dL

Other options:

  • 4 mg/dL, 6 mg/dL → Can cause severe hypocalcemic manifestations but not the classic cutoff used in MCQs

  • 9 mg/dL → Within normal range

Exam pearl:

  • Tetany → Plasma Ca²⁺ < 5 mg/dL

  • Hypocalcemia → Increased neuromuscular excitability

  • Hypercalcemia → Muscle weakness and reduced reflexes

Physiology-04.question: ২৩) Primary sex organ in female
Physiology-04.exp:
The ovary is the primary sex organ (gonad) in females because it produces:

  • Female gametes (ova/eggs)

  • Sex hormones (estrogen and progesterone)

Other female reproductive organs are accessory organs:

  • Uterus → Site of implantation and fetal development

  • Vagina → Birth canal and copulatory organ

  • Fallopian tube → Site of fertilization and transport of ovum

Exam pearl:

  • Primary female sex organ → Ovary

  • Primary male sex organ → Testis

  • Gonads produce gametes + sex hormones

Physiology-04.question: ২৪) Aldosterone is derived from
২৫) Triad of tetany excludes
Physiology-04.exp:
The triad of tetany due to hypocalcemia includes:

  1. Carpopedal spasm → Painful contraction of hands and feet

  2. Stridor → Due to laryngospasm caused by increased neuromuscular excitability

  3. Convulsion → Due to CNS hyperexcitability

Coma is not a feature of tetany triad.

Exam pearl:

  • Tetany triad → Carpopedal spasm + Stridor + Convulsion

  • Hypocalcemia → Increased neuromuscular excitability

  • Hypercalcemia → Muscle weakness, lethargy, decreased reflexes

Physiology-04.question: ২৬) The most active adrenal androgen is
Physiology-04.exp:
The most active androgen produced by the adrenal gland is testosterone (though the adrenal cortex mainly secretes weaker androgen precursors such as DHEA and androstenedione).

Adrenal androgen pathway:

  • DHEA → Weak androgen

  • Androstenedione → Converted to testosterone

  • Testosterone → More biologically active androgen

Other options:

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) → Major adrenal androgen secretion but weak activity

  • Androstenedione → Weak androgen precursor

  • Cortisol → Glucocorticoid, not androgen

Exam pearl:

  • Most abundant adrenal androgen → DHEA

  • Most active androgen → Testosterone

  • Zona reticularis → Adrenal androgens (DHEA)

(Note: Some texts mention DHEA as the principal adrenal androgen because it is the major secreted product; however, when asking “most active androgen,” the answer is Testosterone.)

Physiology-04.question: ২৭) Single best thyroid function test is measurement of
Physiology-04.exp:
The single best thyroid function test is the measurement of serum Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH).

TSH is the most sensitive indicator of thyroid function because:

  • A small change in T3/T4 produces a large reciprocal change in TSH due to negative feedback.

  • It is the best screening test for primary hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism.

Other options:

  • T3 → Less useful as a screening test; may be normal in some hypothyroid states

  • T4 → Useful but less sensitive than TSH

  • FT3 → Mainly useful in suspected T3 toxicosis, not routine screening

Exam pearl:

  • Best initial thyroid function test → Serum TSH

  • Primary hypothyroidism → ↑ TSH + ↓ T4

  • Primary hyperthyroidism → ↓ TSH + ↑ T3/T4

Physiology-04.question: ২৮) D cell f islets of Langerhans secrete
Physiology-04.exp:
The D cells (delta cells) of the islets of Langerhans secrete somatostatin.

Functions of pancreatic islet cells:

  • β (Beta) cells → Insulin (decreases blood glucose)

  • α (Alpha) cells → Glucagon (increases blood glucose)

  • δ (Delta) cells → Somatostatin (inhibits insulin and glucagon secretion)

  • PP/F cells → Pancreatic polypeptide (PP)

Exam pearl:

  • Alpha → Glucagon

  • Beta → Insulin

  • Delta → Somatostatin

  • PP cells → Pancreatic polypeptide

Physiology-04.question: ২৯) GIT effect of hypothyroid state
Physiology-04.exp:
Hypothyroidism causes a decrease in metabolic activity, including reduced gastrointestinal motility, leading to constipation.

GIT effects of hypothyroidism:

  • ↓ Smooth muscle activity

  • ↓ Intestinal peristalsis

  • Constipation (common feature)

Other options:

  • Diarrhoea → More commonly seen in hyperthyroidism due to increased gut motility

  • Vomiting → Not a typical feature

  • Bloating → May occur due to slowed digestion but is not the classic answer

Exam pearl:

  • Hypothyroidism → Constipation

  • Hyperthyroidism → Increased bowel movement/diarrhoea

  • Thyroid hormone generally increases GIT motility.

Physiology-04.question: ৩০) In which ccondition frog like husky voice is found?
Physiology-04.exp:
A frog-like husky voice is a classic feature of myxoedema (adult hypothyroidism) due to mucopolysaccharide deposition and edema of the vocal cords, causing a deep, hoarse voice.

Features of myxoedema:

  • Hoarse/frog-like voice

  • Puffy face

  • Cold intolerance

  • Weight gain

  • Slow speech and mental slowing

  • Dry skin

Other options:

  • Cretinism → Childhood hypothyroidism causing growth retardation and intellectual disability

  • Graves’ disease → Hyperthyroidism; features include weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, exophthalmos

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis → Autoimmune cause of hypothyroidism; may lead to myxoedema but is not the condition described

Exam pearl:

  • Frog-like husky voice → Myxoedema

  • Childhood hypothyroidism → Cretinism

  • Hyperthyroidism → Graves’ disease

Physiology-04.question: ৩১) Functions of insulin excludes
৩২) Most of thyroid hormone is bound to plasma protein...?
Physiology-04.exp:
Most circulating thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) are bound to Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), which is the major plasma transport protein for thyroid hormones.

Plasma binding of thyroid hormones:

  • TBG (Thyroxine-binding globulin) → Binds the largest proportion of T3 and T4 

  • TBPA (Transthyretin/Thyroxine-binding prealbumin) → Binds a smaller amount, especially T4

  • Albumin → Low-affinity but high-capacity binding

  • Fibrinogen → Not involved in thyroid hormone transport

Exam pearl:

  • Major thyroid hormone carrier → TBG

  • T4 is more protein-bound than T3

  • Free T3/T4 are the biologically active forms

Physiology-04.question: ৩৩) Insulin secretion is increased in
৩৪) Which one is secreted from C cell of thyroid?
Physiology-04.exp:
The C cells (parafollicular cells) of the thyroid gland secrete calcitonin.

Functions:

  • Calcitonin decreases blood calcium level by:

    • Inhibiting osteoclast activity

    • Promoting calcium deposition in bone

Thyroid follicular cells secrete:

  • T3 (Triiodothyronine)

  • T4 (Thyroxine)

Other options:

  • T3 → Secreted by follicular cells of thyroid

  • T4/Thyroxine → Secreted by follicular cells of thyroid

  • Calcitonin → Secreted by parafollicular (C) cells 

Exam pearl:

  • Follicular cells → T3 + T4

  • Parafollicular (C) cells → Calcitonin

  • Calcitonin → ↓ Serum Ca²⁺

Physiology-04.question: ৩৫) Pheochromocytoma is a condition characterized by mainly hypersecretion of.........?
Physiology-04.exp:
Pheochromocytoma is a tumor of chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla that causes excessive secretion of catecholamines.

Catecholamines secreted:

  • Epinephrine

  • Norepinephrine

  • Dopamine (less commonly)

Clinical features:

  • Episodic hypertension

  • Headache

  • Sweating

  • Palpitations

  • Tremor

Other options:

  • Glucocorticoids → Produced by zona fasciculata (Cushing syndrome)

  • Mineralocorticoids → Produced by zona glomerulosa (Conn’s syndrome)

  • Sex corticoids → Produced by zona reticularis

Exam pearl:

  • Pheochromocytoma → Adrenal medulla → Catecholamine excess

  • Adrenal cortex → Aldosterone, cortisol, and androgens

Physiology-04.question: ৩৬) Not true about type-1 DM
Physiology-04.exp:
In Type 1 diabetes mellitus, there is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency.

Features of Type 1 DM:

  • Low plasma insulin 

  • Increased plasma glucose (hyperglycemia) 

  • Plasma glucagon resistant to suppression due to lack of insulin-mediated inhibition 

  • Insulin sensitivity is usually normal or increased because insulin resistance is not the primary problem 

Therefore, “Normal insulin sensitivity” is not considered a typical feature in this context.

Exam pearl:

  • Type 1 DM → Absolute insulin deficiency

  • Type 2 DM → Insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency

  • Type 1 DM → ↓ Insulin, ↑ Glucagon, ↑ Ketone formation

Physiology-04.question: ৩৭) Features of gigantism excludes
Physiology-04.exp:
Gigantism occurs due to excess growth hormone (GH) secretion during childhood before epiphyseal plate closure. It causes excessive linear growth.

Features of gigantism:

  • Excessive height 

  • Excessive growth of long bones 

  • Cardiomegaly due to GH excess effects on the heart 

  • Prognathism  (more typical of acromegaly in adults)

In adults, after epiphyseal closure, GH excess causes enlargement of jaw, hands, feet, and facial bones → acromegaly.

Exam pearl:

  • Childhood GH excess → Gigantism → Tall stature

  • Adult GH excess → Acromegaly → Prognathism + enlarged hands/feet

Physiology-04.question: ৩৮) Leydig cell secrets testosterone in stimulation of
৩৯) Which one is not a feature of hyperthyroidism?
Physiology-04.exp:
Hyperthyroidism causes an increase in metabolic rate, leading to increased energy expenditure and weight loss, not weight gain.

Features of hyperthyroidism:

  • Excitability / nervousness 

  • Muscle weakness (especially proximal muscles) 

  • Heat intolerance due to increased heat production 

  • Weight loss due to increased metabolism 

Weight gain is typically a feature of hypothyroidism because of reduced metabolic activity.

Other options:

  • Excitability → Common in hyperthyroidism

  • Muscle weakness → Common due to increased protein catabolism

  • Heat intolerance → Classic feature of hyperthyroidism

Exam pearl:

  • Hyperthyroidism → “Hot, thin, fast”

    • Heat intolerance

    • Weight loss

    • Tachycardia

    • Increased excitability

  • Hypothyroidism → “Cold, slow, fat”

    • Cold intolerance

    • Weight gain

    • Bradycardia

    • Constipation

Physiology-04.question: ৪০) Endocrine secretion of pineal gland
Physiology-04.exp:
The pineal gland is an endocrine gland that secretes melatonin.

Functions of melatonin:

  • Regulates sleep–wake cycle (circadian rhythm)

  • Secretion increases during darkness and decreases in light

  • Influences seasonal reproductive rhythms

Other options:

  • ANP (Atrial natriuretic peptide) → Secreted by cardiac atria

  • HPL (Human placental lactogen) → Secreted by placenta

  • HCG (Human chorionic gonadotropin) → Secreted by placenta

Exam pearl:

  • Pineal gland → Melatonin → Circadian rhythm

  • Melatonin secretion ↑ in darkness

  • Suprachiasmatic nucleus (hypothalamus) → Master biological clock

Physiology-04.question: ৪১) Which one is antidiabetogenic hormone?
Physiology-04.exp:
An antidiabetogenic hormone is a hormone that prevents the development of diabetes by lowering blood glucose levels. The main antidiabetogenic hormone is insulin.

Insulin actions:

  • ↓ Blood glucose level

  • ↑ Glucose uptake by muscle and adipose tissue

  • ↑ Glycogen synthesis

  • ↓ Gluconeogenesis

  • ↓ Glycogenolysis

Other options:

  • Glucagon → Diabetogenic hormone; increases blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis

  • Cortisol → Diabetogenic; increases glucose production and causes insulin resistance

  • Thyroxine → Can increase glucose metabolism and has diabetogenic effects in excess

Exam pearl:

  • Insulin = Antidiabetogenic hormone

  • Glucagon, cortisol, growth hormone, catecholamines, thyroxine = Diabetogenic hormones

Physiology-04.question: ৪২) Fructose as a component of semen if derived from secretion of
৪৩) Which hormone has permissive action?
Physiology-04.exp:
A permissive action means one hormone allows another hormone to exert its full effect. Cortisol has a classic permissive action by enhancing the response of tissues to catecholamines.

Examples:

  • Cortisol ↑ adrenergic receptor expression → increases vascular responsiveness to epinephrine/norepinephrine → maintains normal blood pressure.

  • It also permits actions of glucagon and growth hormone on metabolism.

Other options:

  • Catecholamine → Directly acts through adrenergic receptors, not classically permissive

  • Aldosterone → Regulates sodium and potassium balance

  • ADH → Regulates water reabsorption in kidney

Exam pearl:

  • Classic permissive hormone → Cortisol

  • Cortisol permits catecholamine action on blood vessels

  • Lack of cortisol → reduced response to catecholamines → hypotension in adrenal insufficiency**.**

Physiology-04.question: ৪৪) Lipophilic hormone
Physiology-04.exp:
Lipophilic (lipid-soluble) hormones can cross the cell membrane and bind to intracellular receptors (cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors).

Thyroid hormone (T3 and T4) is lipophilic and acts mainly through nuclear receptors to regulate gene transcription.

Other options:

  • ADH → Hydrophilic peptide hormone; acts via membrane receptors

  • Insulin → Peptide hormone; acts via tyrosine kinase membrane receptors

  • Glucagon → Peptide hormone; acts via GPCR membrane receptors

Exam pearl:

  • Lipophilic hormones → Steroid hormones + Thyroid hormones

  • Hydrophilic hormones → Peptides, proteins, catecholamines

  • Lipophilic → Intracellular receptor

  • Hydrophilic → Cell membrane receptor

Physiology-04.question: ৪৫) Failure of a testes to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum is termed as.......?
Physiology-04.exp:
Cryptorchidism is the condition in which one or both testes fail to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum.

Normal testicular descent:

  • Testes develop in the posterior abdominal wall

  • Descend through the inguinal canal

  • Reach the scrotum before birth

Clinical importance of cryptorchidism:

  • Infertility due to impaired spermatogenesis (higher abdominal temperature)

  • Increased risk of testicular malignancy (especially seminoma)

Other options:

  • Orchitis → Inflammation of the testis

  • Cryptitis → Inflammation of a crypt (not related to testicular descent)

  • Testicular atrophy → Shrinkage of testicular tissue

Exam pearl:

  • Failure of testicular descent → Cryptorchidism

  • Most common site of undescended testis → Inguinal canal

  • Complications → Infertility + testicular cancer

Physiology-04.question: ৪৬) Ovulation occurs at day
৪৭) Which hormone stimulates milk ejection from alveoli into ducts?
Physiology-04.exp:
Oxytocin stimulates milk ejection (let-down reflex) by causing contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli, which pushes milk into the ducts.

Lactation hormones:

  • Prolactin → Stimulates milk production (synthesis) by mammary glands

  • Oxytocin → Stimulates milk ejection from alveoli into ducts 

  • Relaxin → Helps in pregnancy by relaxing pelvic ligaments and softening cervix

  • Inhibin → Inhibits FSH secretion

Exam pearl:

  • Prolactin = Production of milk

  • Oxytocin = Ejection of milk (Let-down reflex)

  • Suckling stimulates both prolactin and oxytocin release.

Physiology-04.question: ৪৮) Which hormone directly control cellular function?
Physiology-04.exp:
Insulin is the hormone that directly controls cellular function by regulating the entry and utilization of glucose inside cells and influencing metabolism.

Actions of insulin:

  • Increases glucose uptake into muscle and adipose cells (via GLUT-4)

  • Promotes glycogen synthesis

  • Promotes fat synthesis (lipogenesis)

  • Promotes protein synthesis

Other options:

  • ADH → Controls water reabsorption in kidney via V2 receptors

  • PTH → Regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism

  • LH → Regulates gonadal hormone production and ovulation

Exam pearl:

  • Insulin = Major hormone controlling cellular metabolism

  • Insulin receptor → Tyrosine kinase receptor

  • Insulin promotes anabolic processes (storage and synthesis)

Physiology-04.question: ৪৯) Which endocrine gland acts without pituitary control?
Physiology-04.exp:
The parathyroid gland acts without pituitary control. Its secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) is regulated directly by serum calcium concentration, not by pituitary hormones.

Regulation:

  • ↓ Blood Ca²⁺ → ↑ PTH secretion

  • ↑ Blood Ca²⁺ → ↓ PTH secretion

Other options:

  • Thyroid → Controlled by TSH from anterior pituitary (for T3/T4 secretion)

  • Adrenal cortex → Mainly controlled by ACTH (especially cortisol secretion)

  • Ovary → Controlled by FSH and LH from anterior pituitary

Exam pearl:

  • Parathyroid = Pituitary-independent endocrine gland

  • PTH regulation → Blood calcium level

  • ↓ Ca²⁺ → ↑ PTH → ↑ serum calcium
